hops.afterHeading: Built wrong, or not kept running?
hops.title: Learning to see after late cataract surgery
hops.text: The early critical-period idea raised doubts that children born blind from cataracts could gain useful sight after the first several years. Project Prakash offered rural Indian children cataract surgery well beyond those years. Surgery sharpened their vision, though it stayed less sharp than usual even a year later. Other skills came online fast. Testing William Molyneux's three-century-old question, researchers asked five patients (four treated for cataracts, one given a corneal transplant) to match a felt shape by sight within 48 hours of surgery; they scored near chance. Three were retested five days, seven days and about five months after their first test, respectively; all three improved.

sources.citation: Sinha P, Held R. Sight restoration. F1000 Medicine Reports 4:17 (2012).
Ganesh S et al. Results of late surgical intervention in children with early-onset bilateral cataracts. British Journal of Ophthalmology 98(10):1424-1428 (2014).
Held R et al. The newly sighted fail to match seen with felt. Nature Neuroscience 14(5):551-553 (2011).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A smooth carved wooden sphere and cube sitting side by side on a sunlit wooden table.
image.caption: Late surgery sharpened vision, though limits stayed; touch-to-sight matching improved in as little as five days after the first test.

hops.afterHeading: Rett syndrome: a circuit that needs MeCP2 to keep running
hops.title: The cloned calico cat who did not match
hops.text: At Texas A&M, 87 transferred embryos yielded one live clone, the first cloned cat, CC (Copy Cat). Her nuclear DNA came from a calico named Rainbow, whose orange and dark patches formed when early cells randomly silenced one X chromosome. Yet CC grew up tabby and white with no orange: identical DNA does not guarantee the same pattern of gene activity. A girl with one mutant MECP2 copy is a mosaic too. In one reported pair of identical twins with Rett syndrome, a DNA marker suggested that the more severely affected twin had the paternal X active in a larger share of the cells sampled.

sources.citation: Randall K. Some Paws For Celebration: World's First Cloned Cat Turns 15 At Texas A&M. Texas A&M Stories (2017).
Shin T et al. A cat cloned by nuclear transplantation. Nature 415:859 (2002).
Ahn JY, Lee JT. X Chromosome: X Inactivation. Nature Education 1(1):24 (2008); Stark LA. CBE Life Sciences Education 9(1):6-9 (2010).
Ishii T et al. The role of different X-inactivation pattern on the variable clinical phenotype with Rett syndrome. Brain & Development 23 Suppl 1:S161-S164 (2001).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A calico cat with orange, black and white patches sitting beside a brown tabby and white cat on a sunny windowsill.
image.caption: CC shared Rainbow's nuclear DNA, yet her coat lacked Rainbow's orange patches.

hops.afterHeading: What mouse models can and cannot show
hops.title: Why lab mice bury marbles
hops.text: For years marble burying was widely read as anxiety: a mouse meets novel objects in its cage and covers them up. In 2009 a team at Baylor College of Medicine tested that idea across ten inbred mouse strains. A strain's burying did not track its scores on two other standard anxiety tests, and letting the mice get used to the marbles first did not change how much they buried. Then the plain control: the same deep bedding, no marbles. The mice dug about as much either way. The authors concluded that marble burying reflects repetitive, persistent digging more than fear of something new.

sources.citation: Thomas A et al. Marble burying reflects a repetitive and perseverative behavior more than novelty-induced anxiety. Psychopharmacology 204(2):361-373 (2009).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A small brown mouse digging into fluffy wood-shaving bedding while two glass marbles sink into the pile behind it.
image.caption: Mice dug about as much without marbles, suggesting burying reflects repetitive digging more than fear of unfamiliar objects.
